events.description: Marxist coup brings PDPA to power in Afghanistan.
Moscow concluded a $250 million military aid agreement with the new regime.
USSR and Afghanistan conclude a friendship treaty.
Uprising in Herat.
General Yepishev visits Kabul.
Moscow deploys eight AN-12s to Afghanistan.
Soviet airborne battalion deployed to Bagram.
Amin assumes control of Defense Ministry and moves Watanjar to Interior Minister.
Brezhnev and Kosygin send a warm message on Afghan independence day.
Pavlovskiy-led delegation secretly visits Kabul to assess Afghan military needs.
Amin seizes sole power, removing Taraki and Watanjar.
Amin assumed effective control of Defense Ministry and appointed Watanjar as Interior Minister.
Brezhnev and Kosygin sent warm message to Afghan leaders for independence day.
Soviet military delegation led by General Pavlovskiy secretly visited Kabul to assess Afghan military needs.
Amin seized sole power, removing Watanjar and Taraki from government.
Soviet battalion introduced to provide security for Bagram airfield.
Amin's seizure of sole power after Taraki's fall; the Soviets view the Kabul situation as unstable.
Four major mutinies in the Afghan Army in the past seven months, plus near-daily small-scale defections.
General Pavlovskiy led a Soviet Ground Forces delegation to Afghanistan to prepare a report on the insurgency and Afghan military.
Clandestine source alleged Soviets had moved about 3,600 combat troops into Kabul (uncorroborated).
Amin's coup in mid-September; seizure of sole power, ousting Taraki.
Marxist government assumed power in Afghanistan (Saur revolution).
Soviet airborne battalion quietly deployed to provide security at Bagram Air Force Base.
Amin seized sole power within the Khalqist regime, displacing Taraki.
Interagency Intelligence Memorandum 'Soviet Options in Afghanistan' finalized with information through 27 September 1979.
Soviets apparently tried and failed to induce the regime to admit other political elements to broaden its base.
A fairly important garrison recently surrendered to the rebels.
Marxist coup brings the PDPA government to power in Afghanistan.
Moscow concluded a $250 million military aid agreement with the new Afghan regime.
General Yepishev visited Kabul in early April, leading to further augmentation of the Soviet military presence.
Moscow deployed eight AN-12s to Afghanistan to transport men and materiel.
An airborne battalion of about 400 Soviet personnel has been at Bagram airbase since early July.
USSR and Afghanistan concluded a friendship treaty, with Article Four on consultation on security.
April 1978 coup in Afghanistan, reference point for credits and Soviet involvement.
USSR and Afghanistan conclude friendship treaty (Article Four consultation on security).
Ambassador Safronchuk told US Charge that Moscow had not persuaded regime to bring new people into government.
Jailed Parcham members in Kabul released at Soviet urging in early July.

East German Ambassador in Kabul claimed Soviets would replace Taraki and Amin by force if necessary (mid-July).
Amin assumed control of Defense Ministry and appointed Watanjar Interior Minister.
Brezhnev and Kosygin sent warm message to Afghan leaders on independence day.
Pavlovskiy-led high-ranking Soviet military delegation secretly visited Kabul for lengthy assessment of Afghan military needs.
Soviet battalion introduced to provide security for Bagram airfield since early July.

key_claims: CIA assessed that Moscow was deferring major new counterinsurgency initiatives pending Amin's consolidation.
CIA believed an airborne battalion of about 400 had been at Bagram since early July 1979.
CIA found no convincing evidence that the Soviets were behind the April 1978 coup.
At least 2,500 Soviet military personnel were in Afghanistan, guiding combat operations.
The Soviets probably did not instigate or foresee Amin's seizure of power in mid-September 1979.
Soviet interests shifted from a friendly buffer state to maintaining a Marxist state.
The CIA judged Moscow had by late August 1979 decided to renew its commitment to the Khalqi leadership and assess military needs, via the Pavlovskiy delegation.
The CIA outlined four Soviet military options, from more equipment and advisers to massive multidivisional intervention.
The CIA assessed that the Soviets probably did not instigate Amin's seizure of power from Taraki.
The CIA believed Moscow would prefer an incremental, minimal increase in role and would deploy airborne divisions to Kabul if control broke down.
An unverified clandestine report claimed 3,600 Soviet combat troops had already moved into Kabul.
Afghan Army loyalty was considered the biggest threat to a holding action, with four mutinies in seven months.
